title: Prizes and Pranks
description: Olympic gold for sculpture, a chimp passed off as a French painter, and Congo the ape artist

concepts.title: Olympic Gold for a Sculpture
concepts.contentHtml:
At the 1912 Olympics in Stockholm, the American marksman Walter Winans won a gold medal for a horse. Not for riding one: for making one. His bronze statuette An American Trotter took the first Olympic gold medal ever awarded for sculpture.1 He was already an Olympic champion with a rifle. Four years earlier in London he had won gold in the running deer event, firing at a moving target.2

The art contests were the dream of Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Games, who believed a true Olympian should be skilled in music and literature as well as sport. For the Games' first four decades, the Olympics gave official medals for painting, sculpture, architecture, literature and music, and every entry had to be inspired by sport. Coubertin even won the 1912 literature gold himself, with an Ode to Sport entered under two pen names, so the jury never knew it was his.3

So why is there no gold for painting today? The contests ran at every Summer Games from 1912 to 1948 and were then dropped because most of the artists were professionals, which the International Olympic Committee opposed.4 Olympians of that era had to be strict amateurs, but artists live by selling their work, and a medal could double as an advertisement. Avery Brundage, a rigid champion of amateur sport who became IOC president, led the campaign against the arts. The 151 art medals were struck from the official record, so they no longer count in any country's tally. One of the last went to Britain's John Copley, aged 73, for an engraving of polo players.5

concepts.title: The Chimp Who Fooled the Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
In February 1964 an art show in Gothenburg, Sweden, hung four paintings by Pierre Brassau, a previously unknown French avant-garde artist.1 Most critics were impressed. One wrote that "Pierre Brassau paints with powerful strokes, but also with clear determination," and that he performed "with the delicacy of a ballet dancer." Another ended a harsh review with a line that turned out to be exactly right: "Only an ape could have done this."2

Pierre Brassau was Peter, a four-year-old chimpanzee from the zoo at Borås. The prank was the idea of Åke "Dacke" Axelsson, a journalist on the Gothenburg daily Göteborgs-Tidningen, who wanted to put the critics to the test: could they tell modern art from monkey art? He persuaded Peter's 17-year-old keeper to give the chimp a brush and oil paints. At first Peter preferred eating the paint, especially the cobalt blue, which is why so much blue ended up in his work. Axelsson then chose the four canvases he thought best.3

When the hoax came out, the critic who had praised Brassau, Rolf Anderberg of the morning paper Posten, stood his ground and insisted the work was "still the best painting in the exhibition."4 One of the paintings had already sold for $90.5

The prank proves less than it seems. The critics were reading color and brushwork, which is what abstract painting asks viewers to do, and the four canvases on the wall had been picked by a human eye. What it shows is how much a name, a backstory and a gallery wall shape what people expect to see.

concepts.title: Congo, the Chimp Collectors Wanted
concepts.contentHtml:
In the mid-1950s the zoologist Desmond Morris, who presented the television show Zoo Time from London Zoo, offered a young chimpanzee named Congo a pencil and a card. "Something strange was coming out of the end of the pencil," Morris wrote at the time. "It was Congo's first line."1

Morris was running an experiment, not a stunt. Congo never drew anything recognizable, but he balanced his marks on the page and favored a radiating fan pattern. He also seemed to know when a picture was done. "If I tried to stop him before he had finished a painting, he would have a screaming fit," Morris recalled, and if pressed to go on after he had finished, "he would stubbornly refuse."2 Between 1956 and 1959 Congo made more than 400 drawings and paintings. In 1957 a selection went on show at the Institute of Contemporary Arts in London, and collectors included Pablo Picasso and Joan Miró.3

Picasso's Congo shows how such stories grow in the retelling. The careful version is that he is reported to have hung a Congo painting on his studio wall after receiving it as a gift.4 Congo died of tuberculosis in 1964. In June 2005 Bonhams in London put three of his paintings into a sale alongside works by Renoir and Warhol. The Renoir and the Warhol failed to sell, while Congo's three went to an American collector for $26,352, against an estimate of $1,000 to $1,500.5

title: Mistakes on the Wall
description: Borja's Ecce Homo, the cartoon St George of Estella, and a Matisse and a Mondrian upside down

concepts.title: Ecce Homo, Ecce Mono
concepts.contentHtml:
On a wall of the Sanctuary of Mercy, a church outside the small town of Borja in northern Spain, hung Ecce Homo, a fresco of Christ crowned with thorns by the painter Elías García Martínez. By the summer of 2012 its paint was flaking badly, and Cecilia Giménez, an 81-year-old parishioner and amateur painter who had touched it up before, volunteered to work on it once again. "I was only trying to do a good thing," she said later, but the paint soaked into the damp and "it got out of control." The new face, with a smudge for a mouth and the beard turned to fur, looked to the world like a monkey, and the internet renamed it Ecce Mono, "Behold the Monkey".1

The mockery hit her hard. "I felt devastated," she told The New York Times. "They said it was a crazy, old woman who destroyed a portrait that was worth a lot of money."2

Then the visitors came. The foundation that owns the sanctuary began charging one euro a head, to cover the extra staff needed to manage the crowds.3 The ticket money goes to the foundation, to improve its facilities and help elderly residents without means at its nursing home, where Giménez herself lived in her last years.4

The town's view turned around. More than 150,000 people came to see the painting in five years, an exhibition center and gift shop opened at the sanctuary, plans to have it professionally restored were dropped, and Giménez sold one of her own landscapes for €1,000 for charity. In 2022 Borja held a gala in her honor for the tenth anniversary. By then she had made peace with her Christ: "I hold it so dear," she said, "to the point that I see him as handsome." She died in December 2025, aged 94.5

concepts.title: St George Turns Into a Cartoon
concepts.contentHtml:
Six years after Borja, it happened again. The church of San Miguel in Estella, in Navarre in northern Spain, has a 16th-century wooden carving of St George on horseback. In 2018 it was repainted in gaudy colors by a local craftsman, when it should have been cleaned by a professional conservator. Fernando Carrera, president of Spain's association of conservator-restorers, said the sculpture "has been turned into a toy."1

Age had darkened the figure to a deep brown. Now the saint had a pink face and a surprised look, and people online compared him to Tintin. Experts took him to an official laboratory in Pamplona, and in 2019, after three months of work and €30,000 paid by the parish, the regional government announced that St George was back to normal. Not quite: some of the original colors were lost forever.2

Why not simply repaint? Old carvings like this are polychrome: painted, sometimes over metal leaf, in layers that record the object's history. A conservator's job is to clean and stabilize those layers, not to cover them. The Navarre team said the finished result would be closest to the paint the figure had in the 18th century, and the culture department opened proceedings to fine both the parish and the crafts company €6,010 each.3

The case revived a Spanish argument about who may touch the nation's heritage. Estella's mayor, Koldo Leoz, called it an example of "the power that churches have over the fate of cultural heritage."4 In 2020, Spanish law still allowed amateurs to repair historic artworks. "Can you imagine just anyone being allowed to operate on other people?" Carrera asked.5

concepts.title: Which Way Is Up?
concepts.contentHtml:
On October 18, 1961, New York's Museum of Modern Art opened a show of Henri Matisse's last cut-paper works. One of them, Le Bateau (1953), a sailboat and its reflection, was hanging upside down. Some 116,000 visitors walked past it, among them Matisse's son Pierre, an art dealer. A stockbroker, Genevieve Habert, was sure: Matisse "would never put the main, more complex motif on the bottom and the lesser motif on top." The guard she told was unmoved: "you don't know what's up and you don't know what's down and neither do we."1

So she called The New York Times, which reported that the picture had hung upside down for 47 days.2 The curator blamed a label stuck upside down on the back. The show closed on December 4, so Le Bateau was the right way up only while it was being taken down.3

A longer case came to light in 2022. Piet Mondrian's New York City I (1941), a lattice of colored adhesive tapes, was first shown at MoMA in 1945 and has hung in Düsseldorf since 1980. The curator Susanne Meyer-Büser noticed the lines thicken toward the bottom. "The thickening of the grid should be at the top, like a dark sky," she said. A similar oil painting in Paris has its dense lines at the top, and a photo taken in Mondrian's studio just after his death shows it the other way up. "I am 100% certain the picture is the wrong way around."4

It will stay as it is, because the tapes are "already extremely loose and hanging by a thread" and turning it could make them slip. Abstract art invites the mistake: with no horizon, faces or figures, the clues are a signature, a label or the artist's working habits, and New York City I is unsigned, perhaps because Mondrian had not finished it.5

title: Art That Isn't There
description: Klein's empty gallery, Rauschenberg's erased de Kooning and Garau's invisible sculpture

concepts.title: Yves Klein Sells the Void
concepts.contentHtml:
In the spring of 1958 a crowd so dense that nobody could move packed a small gallery in Paris. Two Republican Guards in full uniform stood at the door. Inside, there was nothing to look at. Yves Klein had emptied Galerie Iris Clert of exhibits and given its walls several coats of pure white pigment: the empty gallery was itself the exhibit. One visitor shouted that he would come back when the void was full. Klein answered that when it was full, he would no longer be able to get in.1 The show's official title was The Specialization of Sensibility in the Raw Material State of Stabilized Pictorial Sensibility, but it is better known as The Void.2 About 3,000 people lined up to see the empty room.3

Then Klein began selling emptiness itself. From 1959 to 1962 he sold nine zones of immaterial pictorial sensibility: invisible areas of empty space that existed only as an idea, paid for in pure gold. Each buyer got a receipt designed to look like a bank check, and a choice. Keep the receipt, and the zone could be resold like any other artwork. Or burn it in a ritual with the artist, and the zone became part of the buyer, lasting only as long as they lived. Three buyers chose the ritual, in which Klein threw half of the gold into the River Seine. Others kept their receipts, among them the Paris dealer Jacques Kugel, who paid 20 grams of gold for the second zone in 1959.4 In 2022 his receipt sold at Sotheby's in Paris for more than 1.06 million euros.5

The joke and the point are the same. A painting is canvas and pigment, yet its price comes from the name on it, the story behind it and the paperwork that proves who owns it. Klein removed the canvas and pigment, and the rest still worked. The burned receipts went further still, leaving the buyer only a memory.

concepts.title: Erased de Kooning Drawing
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1953 the young painter Robert Rauschenberg set himself an odd problem: could he make a drawing with an eraser? Rubbing out his own drawings did not work. He decided he had to start with a drawing by an artist whose importance nobody could doubt, and his first and only choice was Willem de Kooning, then at the peak of his fame. With great respect and some trepidation, Rauschenberg asked de Kooning for a drawing to erase, and de Kooning, with some reluctance, agreed. Erasing it took considerable time and numerous erasers. Rauschenberg loved telling the story, and it grew over the decades: in later versions de Kooning became more intimidating and the number of erasers went up. De Kooning himself said little. Years later he could not remember whether Rauschenberg had told him what he planned, and called it "sort of a corny idea."1

The finished work is a smudged sheet of paper in a simple gilded frame. Below it, a label lettered by the artist Jasper Johns reads, in three lines: Erased de Kooning Drawing, Robert Rauschenberg, 1953. Without that label, a viewer would have no idea what is in the frame. Was rubbing out a famous artist's work an act of homage, provocation, humor or destruction? Rauschenberg once suggested it was a celebration.2

So what did de Kooning draw? In 2010 SFMOMA, the San Francisco museum that owns the work, scanned the sheet in infrared light and enhanced the image to bring out the faint traces of graphite and charcoal the erasers left behind. The ghost that appeared suggests several figures, drawn from different angles. There is a catch: de Kooning used erasers in his own drawing, so some of the lines in the scan may have been rubbed out by him before Rauschenberg ever touched the sheet.3 The artwork is an absence, and even the absence is hard to read.

concepts.title: Paying for Nothing
concepts.contentHtml:
In May 2021 the Italian auction house Art-Rite sold a sculpture by the artist Salvatore Garau for 15,000 euros, well above its estimate of 6,000 to 9,000 euros. Its title is Io sono, "I am", and there is nothing to see: the work does not exist in any material form. The buyer received a certificate of authenticity signed and stamped by Garau, with instructions to display the work in a clear space about five feet by five feet. Garau defended it with physics, calling a vacuum "nothing more than a space full of energy" and invoking the Heisenberg uncertainty principle to argue that nothing has a weight: a poetic reading of quantum physics rather than a scientific one. He had made invisible works before, including Buddha in Contemplation, marked only by a white square of tape on a walkway in Milan.1 Another, Aphrodite Weeps, stood above a circle of white tape in front of the New York Stock Exchange.2

Not everyone thought Garau was original. Tom Miller, a performance artist in Gainesville, Florida, said he had installed an invisible sculpture called Nothing in the city's Bo Diddley Plaza in 2016. He wanted credit for the idea, and hired an Italian lawyer.3 Invisible art is older than both of them. A 2012 exhibition at London's Hayward Gallery gathered 50 "invisible" works, among them Klein's, Andy Warhol's Invisible Sculpture of 1985, an empty plinth on which he had once briefly stepped, and Tom Friedman's Untitled (A Curse), an empty space cursed by a witch.4

So what does a buyer of nothing own? Mostly paper. The certificate is what turns an invisible sculpture into something that can be owned and sold again, just as Klein's surviving receipt did: because Kugel never burned it, its terms passed his immaterial zone to whoever bought it at auction.5 The price measures belief in the artist and the story, as it partly does for any painting.

title: Priceless Absurdities
description: Manzoni's tins priced in gold, the truth about Van Gogh's ear, and Serra's banished steel wall

concepts.title: Manzoni's Tins: Worth Their Weight in Gold
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1961 the Italian artist Piero Manzoni sealed 90 small tins and signed and numbered each one. He called the work Merda d'artista. A label in Italian, French, German and English says each tin holds 30 grams of the artist's own excrement, "freshly preserved, produced and tinned". Manzoni priced each tin by its weight at that day's market price of gold, which in 1961 came to about $37. Thirty years later Sotheby's auctioned one for $67,000, when the gold rule would have set its price at about $396. Tate in London, which bought No. 4 in 2000, describes its copy as a tin can "with unidentified contents".1 In 2016 No. 69 sold at auction in Milan for 275,000 euros.2

So what is inside? Nobody can say for sure: nothing proves the tins hold what the label claims. In 1989 the French artist Bernard Bazile had one opened in front of invited guests at a gallery in Marseille. Inside was another, much smaller tin, packed in cotton, and the mystery remained.3 In 2007 Agostino Bonalumi, an artist who had worked with Manzoni, wrote in the newspaper Corriere della Sera that the tins held not excrement but plaster.4 His claim, like the label, cannot be checked without opening a tin.

Either way, the work does what Manzoni meant it to. The Centre Pompidou in Paris, which owns No. 31, notes that by selling the tins by weight at the price of gold, Manzoni played with the market value of artworks, and that because the contents are hidden, the viewer has to take the artist's word for it.5 An artist's signature turns an ordinary object into something collectors will pay for. Manzoni pushed that idea as far as it could go, and the market proved his point.

concepts.title: Van Gogh's Ear: What the Doctor Drew
concepts.contentHtml:
In the fall of 1888 Vincent van Gogh, then 35, was sharing the Yellow House in Arles with the painter Paul Gauguin. Their arguments about art grew heated. On December 23, after a fierce quarrel, Vincent cut off his left ear in a state of utter confusion. He wrapped it in paper and took it to a brothel nearby, and the next morning the police found him at home and took him to hospital. Back home two weeks later, he wrote to his brother Theo: "I didn't know that one could break one's brain and that afterwards that got better too."1

How much of the ear did he cut? For over a century accounts clashed; in 2009 two German art historians even argued that Gauguin had sliced off the earlobe with a sword.2 Most historians said only the lobe, trusting the painter Paul Signac, who visited Vincent in hospital and wrote that he had cut off "the lobe" and "not the whole ear". Then the Irish art historian Bernadette Murphy found a 1955 letter at the Van Gogh Museum mentioning a diagram of the wound, drawn by Dr Félix Rey, who treated Vincent, that had ended up with the biographer Irving Stone. An archivist found it among Stone's papers at the University of California, Berkeley, folded in half in a folder of clippings. Vincent had removed the whole ear, leaving only a sliver of the lobe. Signac never saw the ear uncovered: he described Vincent wearing a band around his head and a fur cap.3

The old story got the woman wrong too. Newspapers at the time called her Rachel, and she was long assumed to be a prostitute. Murphy showed she was Gabrielle, an 18-year-old farmer's daughter working as a maid at the brothel. Earlier that year a rabid dog had bitten her, and her family had gone into debt for her treatment in Paris. Murphy promised Gabrielle's descendants she would keep her surname private.4 As for Vincent, more attacks followed. He could later recall nothing of that night, and the cause of his illness is still debated: there are many theories, but no agreed diagnosis.5

concepts.title: Tilted Arc: Voted Off the Plaza
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1979 the US government's General Services Administration (GSA), whose Art in Architecture program set aside half of one percent of the budget of new federal buildings for art, commissioned Richard Serra to make a sculpture for a plaza beside a federal office complex in lower Manhattan, for $175,000. After about a year of reviews, Serra installed Tilted Arc: a curved steel wall 120 feet long and 12 feet high, standing in the middle of Federal Plaza. Office workers loathed it. Two months after it went up, 1,300 federal employees signed a petition asking for its removal. In 1985 the GSA's regional administrator, William Diamond, held a public hearing. Serra argued that the work had been made as a response to that plaza, so that moving it would be "to destroy it."1

The hearing did not go the way you might expect. Of the 180 people who testified, 122 supported the sculpture and 58 favored moving it; opponents compared it to the Berlin Wall. The GSA decided to dismantle it anyway. Serra sued in 1986, but the appeals court ruled that the government had the right to modify, censor or destroy the work. On March 15, 1989, it came down, and Diamond declared: "This is a day for the people to rejoice, because now the plaza returns rightfully to the people."2 Federal workers had cut it into three pieces during the night and carted them off to a scrap-metal yard, eight years after it was installed in 1981.3

Can a government simply remove public art it has paid for? In this case, yes: the government owned it. Since 1990 US law has given artists a little more say, because the Visual Artists Rights Act lets them act to prevent the destruction of a work "of recognized stature".4 The deeper question has no legal answer: a museum painting can be avoided, but a wall across a plaza cannot. Serra wanted to change how people moved through a public space; the people who crossed it daily had the last word.
